34 A length of wire is connected into an electric circuit. The current in the wire is measured.
Which change on its own could increase the current in the wire?
A
an increase in the length of the wire
B
an increase in the radius of the wire
C
an increase in the resistance of the wire
D
an increase in the resistivity of the wire

hints: Notice the circuit supply is unchanged, so the p.d. $V$ across the wire is fixed and current is controlled by $I = V/R$.
Recall how wire resistance depends on geometry and material: $R = \rho L/A$ with area $A = \pi r^2$.
Compare what each listed increase does to $R$: check whether length, area from radius, resistance itself, or resistivity makes $R$ smaller.
walkthrough: Assume the rest of the circuit and e.m.f. are unchanged, so the p.d. $V$ across the wire stays the same and $I = V/R$. To increase $I$ on its own, the wire resistance $R$ must decrease.
Use the resistivity relation $R = \rho L/A$, where $\rho$ is resistivity, $L$ is length and $A$ is cross-sectional area.
Write area in terms of radius: $A = \pi r^2$, so $R = \rho L/(\pi r^2)$. This shows $R$ increases with $L$ and $\rho$, but decreases when $r$ increases.
An increase in length, resistance, or resistivity all make $R$ larger, so $I = V/R$ becomes smaller.
An increase in radius makes $A$ larger, so $R$ becomes smaller and $I = V/R$ becomes larger. This is option B.

A.explanation: Increasing length $L$ increases resistance because $R = \rho L/A$, so for the same p.d. the current $I = V/R$ decreases.

B.explanation: Increasing radius increases cross-sectional area $A = \pi r^2$, which decreases resistance $R = \rho L/A$ and so increases current $I = V/R$.

C.explanation: For a fixed p.d. across the wire, $I = V/R$, so a larger resistance directly gives a smaller current.

D.explanation: Increasing resistivity $\rho$ increases resistance because $R = \rho L/A$, so the current decreases.
